case_name: Parametric ES at 97.5% — Normal P&L (zero mean)
computation: ES formula for normal: ES_α = μ + σ × φ(Φ⁻¹(α))/(1−α). With μ=0: ES_α = σ × φ(z_α)/(1−α)
VaR_α = μ + σ × Φ⁻¹(α) = σ × z_α (zero mean)
formula_basis: ES_α = μ + σ·φ(Φ⁻¹(α))/(1−α) for X ~ N(μ,σ²) (parametric ES under normality). VaR_α = μ + σ·Φ⁻¹(α). The ES multiplier φ(z)/(1−α) is the tail-integral factor; VaR uses only the quantile z. BCBS MAR33.4 establishes 97.5% ES as the FRTB market risk capital standard; the parametric normal approach applies this formula directly. The essential distinction: VaR is a quantile, ES is the mean of the entire tail beyond the quantile — hence the ES multiplier exceeds the VaR multiplier.
weakest_point: The normality assumption is the fundamental limitation: real trading P&L exhibits fat tails (kurtosis > 3), so parametric ES under normality underestimates true tail risk. φ(1.9600) is specified to 4 decimals (0.05844); the exact value 0.058439 changes the ES multiplier by 0.000004 — negligible at portfolio scale but worth noting for exactness. The ES-vs-VaR distinction is exact here: VaR is the 97.5% quantile (1.96σ), ES is the mean of everything beyond (2.3376σ); conflating them would be the defect this case exists to catch.

case_name: Parametric ES at 99% — Normal P&L (zero mean)
computation: ES formula (normal, μ=0): ES_α = σ × φ(Φ⁻¹(α))/(1−α)
formula_basis: Same parametric normal ES as Case 1, at α=99%. ES_α = σ·φ(Φ⁻¹(α))/(1−α). At 99% the tail is thinner (1% vs 2.5%), so the ES multiplier (2.665) is higher than VaR (2.3263), but the ES/VaR ratio (1.1456) is lower than at 97.5% (1.1927) — a property of the normal distribution where extreme tail averages converge toward the quantile as α→1. Under fat-tailed distributions this ratio would increase, not decrease — a key diagnostic that the normal assumption is strained at extreme quantiles.
weakest_point: At 99% the ES multiplier is more sensitive to φ precision: using φ=0.026652 (exact) gives ES multiplier 2.6652 vs 2.6650 — a 0.0002 difference. The normality assumption is more problematic at 99%; real tail behavior diverges sharply from normal at extreme quantiles. The ES/VaR ratio decreasing from 1.1927 (97.5%) to 1.1456 (99%) is correct for normal but would reverse for fat-tailed distributions — this inversion is itself a diagnostic that the parametric normal model is understating tail risk at high confidence levels.

case_name: Liquidity-horizon-scaled ES — Credit spread risk (high yield)

inputs.liquidity_horizon: LH = 120 days (per FRTB liquidity horizon grid)

computation: Step 1: Compute 10-day parametric ES (97.5%) for this risk factor
σ_10 = $8M (10-day P&L volatility for this risk factor)
Step 2: Apply liquidity horizon scaling per MAR33
formula_basis: ES_scaled = ES_10day × √(LH/10). BCBS MAR33.6-33.9 assigns each risk factor category a liquidity horizon LH (10 to 120 days, based on market liquidity characteristics) and scales the 10-day ES by √(LH/10) to capture the longer unwinding period in stressed markets. The square-root scaling follows the standard time-scaling rule for volatility under i.i.d. assumptions. High-yield credit spreads are assigned LH=120 days in the regulatory grid.
weakest_point: The √(LH/10) scaling inherits the i.i.d.-normality assumption: the square-root-of-time rule is exact for volatility under i.i.d. normality but approximate for ES, which is a tail measure not governed by the same scaling. Additionally, the FRTB liquidity horizon grid is coarse (all high-yield credit spreads → 120 days regardless of instrument-specific liquidity), and the 10-day ES input ($18.70M) itself carries all the parametric normality-model risk from Cases 1-2. The scaled ES compounds both uncertainties.

computation: Step 1: Sort P&L observations from worst (most negative) to best (most positive)
Step 2: Determine number of observations in the 97.5% tail
CONVENTION: Ceiling of expected tail count
This is the 'minimum tail' convention — take the worst k observations where k is the
ceiling of the expected count. It is simple, conservative (includes the worst observation),
and commonly used in practice for small-sample ES.
NOTE ON FRACTIONAL OBSERVATIONS (stated honestly as a convention):
The FRTB text (BCBS MAR33) is silent on how to handle fractional tail counts.
Alternative conventions exist and would change the result:
• Floor convention: k = ⌊0.5⌋ = 0 — ES undefined (no observations in tail)
• Interpolation: weight the worst observation by 0.5 and second-worst by 0.5,
• Ceiling convention (used here): k = ⌈0.5⌉ = 1, ES = −12.5 → $12.50M loss
With n=20, the choice between ceiling and interpolation changes ES by $0.35M.
Step 4: Compute ES as the average of the tail observations
Observations ENTERING the 97.5% tail: Rank 1 only (−12.5)
Observations NOT in tail: Ranks 2-20 (all others)
formula_basis: Empirical ES_α = (1/k) × Σ_{i=1}^{k} x_(i) where x_(i) are sorted P&L observations (worst first) and k = ⌈(1−α)n⌉ under the ceiling convention for fractional observations. BCBS MAR33 defines historical-simulation ES as the average of the worst (1−α)% of P&L observations. With n=20 and α=97.5%, expected tail size is 0.5 observations; the regulatory text does not specify how to handle this fractional case, so the ceiling convention is applied and named explicitly.
weakest_point: The sample size (n=20) is critically small for ES estimation — only 1 observation enters the tail, making ES equal to a single data point (the sample minimum) rather than a robust tail average. The ceiling convention (k=1) was chosen over interpolation (which would give $12.15M, a $0.35M difference); the choice materially affects the result. With n=20, the 97.5% ES is barely distinguishable from the sample minimum — this illustrates why FRTB's historical simulation approach requires much larger samples (typically 250+ daily observations) to produce reliable tail estimates. The result is statistically fragile and convention-dependent.
